title: The wealth that sees
source_text: Ἐὰν οὖν ἡ λέξις τοῦ νόμου πλοῦτον ἐπαγγέλλεται τοῖς δικαίοις, Κέλσος μὲν κατὰ τὸ ἀποκτέννον „γράμμα“ νομιζέτω τὸν τυφλὸν πλοῦτον λέγεσθαι ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ· ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸν ὀξὺ βλέποντα, καθὸ πλουτεῖ τις „ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ πάσῃ γνώσει,“ καὶ καθὸ παραγγέλλομεν „τοῖς πλουσίοις ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι μὴ ὑψηλὰ φρονεῖν μηδ᾿ ἠλπικέναι ἐπὶ πλούτου ἀδηλότητι ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ θεῷ, τῷ παρέχοντι πάντα πλουσίως εἰς ἀπόλαυσιν, ἀγαθοεργεῖν, πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς, εὐμεταδότους εἶναι, κοινωνικούς.“ καὶ γὰρ „ὁ“ ἐν ἀληθινοῖς ἀγαθοῖς „πλοῦτος“ „λύτρον ἐστὶν ἀνδρὸς ψυχῆς“ κατὰ τὸν Σολομῶντα, ἡ δ᾿ ἐναντία τούτῳ πτωχεία ὀλέθριον, δι᾿ ἣν „ὁ πτωχὸς οὐχ ὑφίσταται ἀπειλήν.“ ἀνάλογον δὲ τοῖς ἀποδεδομένοις περὶ τοῦ πλούτου λεκτέον καὶ περὶ τῆς δυναστείας, καθ᾿ ἣν „εἷς“ δίκαιος διώξεσθαι λέγεται „χιλίους, καὶ δύο“ μετακινεῖν „μυριάδας.“ εἴπερ δὲ ταῦτα νενόηται ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον, ὅρα εἰ μὴ ἀκόλουθόν ἐστιν ἐπαγγελίᾳ θεοῦ τὸν πλουτοῦντα „ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ πάσῃ γνώσει“ καὶ πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ δανείζειν ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ τὸν λόγον καὶ τὴν σοφίαν καὶ τὴν γνῶσιν πλούτου „ἔθνεσι πολλοῖς,“ ὡς ἐδάνεισε Παῦλος „κύκλῳ“ „ἀπὸ Ἱερουσαλὴμ“ ἕως „τοῦ Ἰλλυρικοῦ“ πληρῶν „τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ“ πᾶσιν ἔθνεσιν, οἷς ἐπιδεδήμηκε. καὶ ἐπεὶ κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν αὐτῷ ἐγνωρίζετο τὰ θεῖα, φωτιζομένῳ τὴν ψυχὴν ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ λόγου θειότητος, διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸς οὐκ ἐδανείζετο οὐδὲ χρείαν εἶχεν ἀνθρώπου διακονουμένου αὐτῷ τὸν λόγον. οὕτω δὲ γεγραμμένου καὶ τοῦ· „ἄρξεις σὺ ἐθνῶν πολλῶν, σοῦ δὲ οὐκ ἄρξουσι,“ κατὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου δυναστείαν ὑποτάσσων τῇ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίᾳ τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν ἦρχεν αὐτῶν, οὐδέ ποτε ἐν χώρᾳ ὑποτεταγμένος ἀνθρώποις ὡς κρείττοσι γινομένοις· οὕτω δὲ καὶ κατεπίμπλα τὴν γῆν.
pass_a_gloss: If then the wording (λέξις) of the law promises (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) wealth (πλοῦτος) to the just, let Celsus according to the killing (ἀποκτείνω) letter (γράμμα) think the blind (τυφλός) wealth to be spoken in promise (ἐπαγγελία); but we [think] the sharp-seeing (ὀξὺ βλέπων) [wealth], according to which one is rich (πλουτέω) in all speech (λόγος) and all knowledge (γνῶσις), and according to which we charge (παραγγέλλω) the rich in the present age (αἰών) not to think high things (ὑψηλὰ φρονεῖν) nor to have hoped (ἐλπίζω) on the uncertainty (ἀδηλότης) of wealth but on God, the one providing (παρέχω) all things richly (πλουσίως) for enjoyment (ἀπόλαυσις), to do good (ἀγαθοεργέω), to be rich in good works (ἔργα ἀγαθά), to be generous (εὐμετάδοτος), sharing (κοινωνικός). For the wealth in true goods (ἀληθινὰ ἀγαθά) is ransom (λύτρον) of a man's soul (ψυχή) according to Solomon, but the poverty (πτωχεία) contrary to this [is] ruinous (ὀλέθριος), through which the poor (πτωχός) does not withstand (ὑφίσταμαι) threat (ἀπειλή). Analogously (ἀνάλογον) to what has been rendered (ἀποδίδωμι) about wealth it must be said also about power (δυναστεία), according to which one just man is said to pursue (διώκω) a thousand, and two to move away (μετακινέω) myriads (μυριάδες). If these things have been understood in the [sayings] about wealth, see whether it is not consequent (ἀκόλουθον) to God's promise that the one rich in all speech and all knowledge and all wisdom (σοφία) and in every good work lends (δανείζω) from the wealth according to the word/reason (λόγος) and wisdom and knowledge to many nations, as Paul lent, round about (κύκλῳ) from Jerusalem to Illyricum, fulfilling (πληρόω) the gospel (εὐαγγέλιον) of Christ to all nations to which he had come (ἐπιδημέω). And since according to revelation (ἀποκάλυψις) divine things (τὰ θεῖα) were made known (γνωρίζω) to him, enlightened (φωτίζω) in the soul by the divinity (θειότης) of the Word (λόγος), for this he himself did not borrow nor had need (χρεία) of a man ministering (διακονέω) the word to him. And it being written thus also: 'you will rule (ἄρχω) many nations, but they will not rule you', according to the power (δυναστεία) from the word, subjecting (ὑποτάσσω) to the teaching (διδασκαλία) of Christ Jesus those from the nations he ruled them, never in the place (χώρα) of being subjected to men as to [those] becoming stronger/better (κρείττονες); and so he filled up (καταπίμπλημι) the earth.
pass_b_english: If, then, the wording of the law promises wealth to the righteous, let Celsus, following the “letter” that kills (2 Corinthians 3:6), suppose that the promise speaks of blind wealth; but we take it to mean the wealth that sees sharply (Plato, Laws 631c): the wealth by which a man is rich “in all speech and all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:5), and the wealth meant when we charge “those who are rich in this present age not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides all things for enjoyment; to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous, ready to share” (1 Timothy 6:17–18). For “the wealth” that consists in true goods “is the ransom of a man’s soul”, according to Solomon, while the poverty opposed to it is ruinous; because of it “the poor man does not stand up to a threat” (Proverbs 13:8).

We must speak about dominion in the same way as we have spoken about wealth: the dominion by which “one” righteous man is said to pursue “a thousand, and two” to put “tens of thousands” to flight (Deuteronomy 32:30). If this is how the passages about wealth are understood, see whether it is not in keeping with God’s promise that the man who is rich “in all speech and all knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1:5), and in all wisdom, and in every good work, lends “to many nations” (Deuteronomy 15:6) out of his wealth in the word and in wisdom and knowledge, just as Paul lent when, “from Jerusalem and round about” as far as “Illyricum”, he fully preached “the gospel of Christ” (Romans 15:19) to all the nations he visited. And since divine things were made known to him by revelation (Ephesians 3:3), his soul being enlightened by the divinity of the Word, for this reason he himself did not borrow, nor did he need any man to minister the word to him.

And since it is also written in the same way, “You shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you” (Deuteronomy 15:6), Paul, by the dominion that comes from the word, brought those from the nations under the teaching of Christ Jesus and ruled over them, never standing in the place of one subject to men as though they were his betters. In this way, too, he filled the earth.

choices.choice: ‘Blind wealth’ versus ‘wealth that sees sharply’ (τυφλὸς / ὀξὺ βλέπων) echoes Plato, Laws 631c, where wealth ‘not blind but sharp-sighted, if it follows wisdom’ is ranked among the human goods; cited inline as the source of the contrast. 1 Timothy 6:17: Origen omits ἡμῖν after παρέχοντι; the rendering follows Origen’s wording (‘provides all things for enjoyment’) and does not restore ‘us’. Proverbs 13:8 LXX: λύτρον ἀνδρὸς ψυχῆς ὁ ἴδιος πλοῦτος, πτωχὸς δὲ οὐχ ὑφίσταται ἀπειλήν; Origen inserts ‘in true goods’ and recasts the sentence, so his insertion stands outside the quotation marks. Deuteronomy 32:30 LXX (εἷς χιλίους, καὶ δύο μετακινήσουσιν μυριάδας) fits Origen’s μετακινεῖν better than Leviticus 26:8; μετακινεῖν μυριάδας rendered ‘put tens of thousands to flight’. ‘In every good work’ may echo 2 Corinthians 9:8; not cited. Romans 15:19: Origen’s ‘to all the nations he visited’ is his own addition. κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν αὐτῷ ἐγνωρίζετο matches the wording of Ephesians 3:3 (κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν ἐγνωρίσθη μοι, ‘by revelation was made known to me’), so Ephesians 3:3 is cited; the thought that Paul ‘did not borrow ... nor need any man to minister the word to him’ also recalls Galatians 1:12 and 1:16–17 (his gospel came by revelation, and he did not consult flesh and blood). δυναστεία rendered ‘dominion’ throughout the chapter, including ‘the dominion that comes from the word’. θειότης τοῦ λόγου capitalised ‘the Word’ (the divine Logos); the other λόγος uses here (wealth ‘in the word’, ‘the word’ ministered, ‘the power that comes from the word’) are taken as the message or reason and kept lowercase, though ‘the word’ in the last paragraph could also be read as the Word. ‘Filled the earth’ turns Celsus’s charge in 7.18 (‘to fill the earth’) to Paul’s preaching. ὡς κρείττοσι γινομένοις rendered ‘as though they were his betters’.
second καθό: 'by which we charge' (wrong sense) -> 'the wealth meant when we charge'
'In the same way as what has been set out about wealth' reordered: 'We must speak about dominion in the same way as we have spoken about wealth'
εἴπερ ταῦτα νενόηται ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον: 'If these things are understood as in the case of wealth' -> 'If this is how the passages about wealth are understood'
ἀκόλουθόν ἐστιν ἐπαγγελίᾳ θεοῦ: 'follow from God's promise' -> 'in keeping with God's promise'
ὡς ἐδάνεισε Παῦλος rejoined to its sentence ('just as Paul lent')
citation Galatians 1:12 -> Ephesians 3:3, whose wording Origen reproduces (κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν ἐγνωρίσθη μοι); bible_refs updated
δυναστεία: 'the power that comes from the word' -> 'the dominion that comes from the word' (consistent with the chapter)
citations checked: 2 Corinthians 3:6, Plato Laws 631c, 1 Corinthians 1:5, 1 Timothy 6:17-18, Proverbs 13:8, Deuteronomy 32:30, Deuteronomy 15:6, Romans 15:19
